cards.title: Data lives in tables
cards.text: A database keeps its data in tables, like sheets in Excel. Northwind is a small food company; its table **products** lists what it sells, one product per row.

columns.name: product_id
columns.about: the number of the product. Every product has its own.

columns.name: units_in_stock
columns.about: how many units are in the warehouse.

cards.after: Each column has a name. In a query you ask for data by these names.

cards.title: SELECT picks the columns
cards.text: A query asks the database for data. `select` says which columns to show, `from` says which table to take them from.

query.postgres:
select product_name, unit_price
from products;

cards.after: You get all 77 products, but only the two columns you asked for.
cards.tip: Want every column? Write `select *`.

cards.title: WHERE filters the rows
cards.text: `where` is a filter: only the rows that match the condition stay. Here the condition is `unit_price > 50`, so only products that cost more than 50 are left.
cards.after: Only 7 products cost more than 50.
cards.tip: Two conditions: `and` means both must be true, `or` means one is enough.

cards.title: ORDER BY sorts the rows
cards.text: `order by` sorts the rows by a column. Here `order by unit_price desc` puts the most expensive first: `desc` means from big to small.

query.postgres:
select product_name, unit_price
from products
where unit_price > 50
order by unit_price desc;

cards.after: Now the most expensive product is at the top.
cards.tip: Without `desc` it sorts from small to big. Without `order by` the database may return rows in any order.

cards.title: LIMIT keeps the first rows
cards.text: `limit` keeps only the first rows of the result. Here we sort by price, most expensive first, and keep 3.

query.postgres:
select product_name, unit_price
from products
order by unit_price desc
limit 3;

cards.after: The 3 most expensive products.
cards.tip: Sort before `limit`: without `order by`, "the first 3" can be any 3.

cards.title: OFFSET skips rows
cards.text: `offset` skips rows from the top. `limit 3 offset 3` skips the first 3 and shows the next 3, like page 2 of a list.

query.postgres:
select product_name, unit_price
from products
order by unit_price desc
limit 3 offset 3;

cards.after: Products 4, 5 and 6 by price.
cards.tip: PostgreSQL also knows the standard spelling `fetch first 3 rows only`; MySQL has only `limit`.

cards.title: Values repeat
cards.text: Here each row is one customer, and many customers are in the same country. So the same country shows up many times.
cards.after: 91 rows, one per customer, with lots of repeats.

cards.title: DISTINCT removes repeats
cards.text: `select distinct` removes repeats: each value shows up only once. Here each country appears once.
cards.after: 21 different countries.
cards.tip: With several columns, a row counts as a repeat only when all its columns are the same.

cards.title: NULL: no value
cards.text: **NULL** means "no value": nobody filled this cell in. It is not 0 and not an empty text, it is simply unknown.
cards.after: Many customers have no region, so their cell says NULL.

cards.title: IS NULL finds them
cards.text: To find cells with no value, write `where region is null`. Careful: `= null` finds nothing, because SQL cannot compare anything with an unknown value.

query.postgres:
select company_name
from customers
where region is null
order by customer_id;

cards.after: 60 customers have no region.
cards.tip: The opposite, `is not null`, keeps the rows that do have a value.

cards.title: COALESCE fills the gaps
cards.text: `coalesce` puts a value in place of NULL. Here `coalesce(region, 'none')` shows the region, or the word none when there is no region.

query.postgres:
select company_name,
  coalesce(region, 'none') as region
from customers
order by customer_id;

cards.after: No NULLs left: the missing regions now say none.

cards.title: LIKE searches by a pattern
cards.text: `like` finds texts that fit a pattern. In the pattern `%` means "any text here", so `'Ch%'` finds names that start with Ch.

query.postgres:
select product_name
from products
where product_name like 'Ch%'
order by product_id;

cards.after: 6 product names start with Ch.
cards.tip: `_` means exactly one character: `'_hai'` finds Chai.

cards.title: Anywhere in the text
cards.text: `%` on both sides finds the word anywhere in the text. `ilike` works like `like`, but does not care about capital letters.

query.postgres:
select product_name
from products
where product_name ilike '%sauce%'
order by product_id;
query.mysql:
select product_name
from products
where product_name like '%sauce%'
order by product_id;

cards.after: 2 products have "sauce" in the name, even though it is written with a capital S.
cards.tip: MySQL has no `ilike`, but there `like` usually ignores capital letters already.
cards.mysqlText: `%` on both sides finds the word anywhere in the text. In MySQL `like` usually does not care about capital letters.
cards.mysqlTip: In PostgreSQL `like` does care about capital letters: there you write `ilike` instead.

cards.title: IN: one of a list
cards.text: `in` checks if a value is in a list. `country in ('UK', 'France')` is a short way to write `country = 'UK' or country = 'France'`.

query.postgres:
select company_name, country
from customers
where country in ('UK', 'France')
order by customer_id;

cards.after: 18 customers are in the UK or France.

cards.title: BETWEEN: a range
cards.text: `between` keeps values in a range. `between 10 and 20` means from 10 to 20, and 10 and 20 themselves count too.

query.postgres:
select product_name, unit_price
from products
where unit_price between 10 and 20
order by unit_price, product_id;

cards.after: 29 products cost from 10 to 20.

cards.title: CASE: a label for each row
cards.text: `case` gives each row a label by rules. It checks the `when` lines from the top and uses the first one that is true; `else` is for all the rest.

query.postgres:
select product_name, unit_price,
  case
    when unit_price > 50 then 'high'
    when unit_price > 20 then 'mid'
    else 'low'
  end as price_level
from products
order by product_id;

cards.after: Every product now has a price label: high, mid or low.

cards.title: Gluing text together
cards.text: `||` glues texts together. Here `city || ', ' || country` turns two columns into one text, with a comma and a space between them.

query.postgres:
select company_name,
  city || ', ' || country
    as place
from customers
order by customer_id;
query.mysql:
select company_name,
  concat(city, ', ', country)
    as place
from customers
order by customer_id;

cards.after: Two columns turned into one.
cards.tip: In MySQL `||` means OR: use `concat()` there. PostgreSQL has `concat()` too.
cards.mysqlText: `concat()` glues texts together. Here `concat(city, ', ', country)` turns two columns into one text, with a comma and a space between them.
cards.mysqlTip: Careful: in MySQL `||` means OR. PostgreSQL glues texts with `||`.

cards.title: Changing text
cards.text: `lower()` writes a text in small letters, `upper()` in capitals. `length()` counts its characters.

query.postgres:
select product_name,
  lower(product_name) as small,
  length(product_name) as len
from products
order by product_id;
query.mysql:
select product_name,
  lower(product_name) as small,
  char_length(product_name) as len
from products
order by product_id;

cards.tip: In MySQL `length()` counts bytes, so é counts twice: use `char_length()`.
cards.mysqlText: `lower()` writes a text in small letters, `upper()` in capitals. `char_length()` counts its characters.
cards.mysqlTip: In MySQL `length()` counts bytes, so é counts twice.

cards.title: Math on columns
cards.text: You can do math with columns, like on a calculator. Here price × units in stock gives what the stock is worth; `as` names the new column.

query.postgres:
select unit_price, units_in_stock,
  unit_price * units_in_stock
    as stock_value
from products
order by product_id;

cards.after: The new column is worked out for every row.

cards.title: Rounding
cards.text: `round(x, 2)` rounds a number to two digits after the point, like money. Here it tidies up the price with 17% tax added (`* 1.17`).

query.postgres:
select unit_price,
  round(unit_price * 1.17, 2)
    as with_tax
from products
order by product_id;

cards.title: Whole numbers divide whole
cards.text: In PostgreSQL `7 / 2` gives 3, not 3.5: when both numbers are whole, the answer is whole too. Write `7 / 2.0` to get 3.5. `%` gives what is left over.
cards.tip: In MySQL `/` always keeps the fraction; `div` divides whole numbers.
cards.mysqlText: In MySQL `7 / 2` gives 3.5. To divide without the fraction, write `7 div 2`: that gives 3. `%` gives what is left over.
cards.mysqlTip: In PostgreSQL `7 / 2` gives 3: whole numbers divide whole there.

cards.title: Parts of a date
cards.text: `extract` takes one part out of a date. Here `extract(year from order_date)` gives just the year; it works with `month` and `day` too.

query.postgres:
select order_date,
  extract(year from order_date)
    as order_year
from orders
order by order_id;

cards.after: Now you could count the orders of each year.

cards.title: Moving a date
cards.text: To move a date, add an interval. Here `order_date + interval '7 days'` gives the date one week after the order.

query.postgres:
select order_date,
  order_date + interval '7 days'
    as week_later
from orders
order by order_id;
query.mysql:
select order_date,
  date_add(order_date,
           interval 7 day)
    as week_later
from orders
order by order_id;

cards.tip: MySQL writes it `date_add(order_date, interval 7 day)`.
cards.mysqlText: `date_add` moves a date. Here `date_add(order_date, interval 7 day)` gives the date one week after the order.

cards.title: Tables are linked
cards.text: Data is split across tables. Each product has a **category_id**: the number of its row in **categories**. That number links the two tables.

columns.name: category_id
columns.about: the number of the product's category: find it in **categories**.

columns.name: category_id
columns.about: the number of the category. Products point to it.

cards.after: Chai has category_id 1, and row 1 of categories is Beverages: Chai is a drink.

cards.title: JOIN puts linked rows together
cards.text: `join` glues each row to its partner in another table. `on` says which columns must match: here the category_id of the product and of the category.

query.postgres:
select p.product_name,
  c.category_name
from products p
join categories c
  on c.category_id = p.category_id
order by p.product_id;

cards.after: Every product now has its category name next to it.
cards.tip: `p` and `c` are short names for the tables, so `p.product_name` means "product_name of products".

cards.title: JOIN drops rows without a partner
cards.text: With `join`, a row that has no partner disappears. Customer FISSA has never ordered anything, GROSR has.

query.postgres:
select c.customer_id, o.order_id
from customers c
join orders o
  on o.customer_id = c.customer_id
where c.customer_id
  in ('FISSA', 'GROSR')
order by c.customer_id, o.order_id;

cards.after: Only the 2 orders of GROSR are here. FISSA is gone.

cards.title: LEFT JOIN keeps them
cards.text: `left join` keeps every row of the first table. Where there is no partner, the columns of the other table are NULL.

query.postgres:
select c.customer_id, o.order_id
from customers c
left join orders o
  on o.customer_id = c.customer_id
where c.customer_id
  in ('FISSA', 'GROSR')
order by c.customer_id, o.order_id;

cards.after: FISSA is back, with NULL where its order would be.
cards.tip: `right join` is the same the other way round: it keeps every row of the second table.

cards.title: FULL JOIN keeps both sides
cards.text: `full join` keeps the rows without a partner from both tables. Here: countries with customers but no suppliers, and countries with suppliers but no customers.

query.postgres:
select distinct
  c.country as customers,
  s.country as suppliers
from customers c
full join suppliers s
  on s.country = c.country
where c.country is null
   or s.country is null
order by suppliers, customers;
query.mysql:
select c.country as customers,
  s.country as suppliers
from customers c
left join suppliers s
  on s.country = c.country
where s.country is null
union
select c.country, s.country
from customers c
right join suppliers s
  on s.country = c.country
where c.country is null;

cards.after: 13 countries have only one side: the other column is NULL.
cards.tip: MySQL has no `full join`: there you glue a `left join` and a `right join` with `union`.
cards.mysqlText: A full join keeps the rows without a partner from both tables. MySQL has no `full join`, so here a `left join` and a `right join` are glued with `union`.
cards.mysqlTip: PostgreSQL writes it in one go: `customers c full join suppliers s on …`.

cards.title: A table joined to itself
cards.text: Each employee has **reports_to**: the employee_id of their manager, in the same table. Join the table to itself under two names: `e` for the employee, `m` for the manager.

query.postgres:
select e.last_name,
  m.last_name as manager
from employees e
join employees m
  on m.employee_id = e.reports_to
order by e.employee_id;

cards.after: 8 employees have a manager. The top boss has none, so `join` leaves them out.

cards.title: CROSS JOIN: every pair
cards.text: `cross join` pairs every row of one table with every row of the other, with no `on`. Useful when you need all combinations.

query.postgres:
select e.last_name, c.category_name
from employees e
cross join categories c
order by e.employee_id,
  c.category_id;

cards.after: 72 rows: every employee with every category.

cards.title: GROUP BY makes groups
cards.text: `group by country` puts the customers of each country into one group, and the result has one row per group. `count(*)` counts the rows of each group.

query.postgres:
select country,
  count(*) as customers
from customers
group by country
order by country;

cards.after: 21 countries, one row each.
cards.tip: Every column in `select` must either be in `group by` or sit inside `count()`, `sum()` and the like.

cards.title: HAVING filters the groups
cards.text: `where` filters rows before grouping; `having` filters the groups after. Here only countries with at least 5 customers stay.

query.postgres:
select country,
  count(*) as customers
from customers
group by country
having count(*) >= 5
order by country;

cards.after: 7 countries have 5 or more customers.

cards.title: Many rows into one number
cards.text: `count` counts rows, `sum` adds up, `avg` gives the average, `min` and `max` the smallest and the biggest. Here: one row about all the products.

query.postgres:
select count(*) as products,
  sum(units_in_stock) as stock,
  max(unit_price) as top_price,
  round(avg(unit_price), 2)
    as avg_price
from products;

cards.tip: With `group by`, you get these numbers for each group instead of for the whole table.

cards.title: Counting different values
cards.text: `count(distinct x)` counts each different value once. Here: how many orders there are, and how many different customers placed them.

query.postgres:
select count(*) as orders,
  count(distinct customer_id)
    as customers
from orders;

cards.title: Many values into one text
cards.text: `string_agg` glues the values of a group into one text, with a separator between them. Here: the last names of the employees with each job title.

query.postgres:
select title,
  string_agg(last_name, ', '
    order by last_name) as names
from employees
group by title
order by title;
query.mysql:
select title,
  group_concat(last_name
    order by last_name
    separator ', ') as names
from employees
group by title
order by title;
rows: Davolio, Dodsworth, King, Leverling, Peacock, Suyama

cards.tip: MySQL calls it `group_concat(x separator ', ')`.
cards.mysqlText: `group_concat` glues the values of a group into one text, with a separator between them. Here: the last names of the employees with each job title.

cards.title: Counting only some rows
cards.text: `count(*) filter (where …)` counts only the rows that match. Here, for each employee: all their orders, and the big ones with freight over 100.

query.postgres:
select employee_id,
  count(*) as orders,
  count(*) filter
    (where freight > 100) as big
from orders
group by employee_id
order by employee_id;
query.mysql:
select employee_id,
  count(*) as orders,
  sum(case when freight > 100
      then 1 else 0 end) as big
from orders
group by employee_id
order by employee_id;

cards.after: Two counts side by side, in one query.
cards.tip: MySQL has no `filter`: `sum(case when … then 1 else 0 end)` adds 1 for each matching row.
cards.mysqlText: `sum(case when … then 1 else 0 end)` adds 1 for each matching row, so it counts only those. Here, for each employee: all orders, and the ones with freight over 100.
cards.mysqlTip: PostgreSQL can also write it `count(*) filter (where freight > 100)`.

cards.title: UNION stacks results
cards.text: `union` puts the rows of two queries one under the other and removes repeats. Here: every country that has a customer or a supplier.

query.postgres:
select country from customers
union
select country from suppliers
order by country;

cards.after: 25 countries in all.
cards.tip: `union all` keeps the repeats, and is faster.

cards.title: EXCEPT and INTERSECT
cards.text: `except` keeps the rows of the first query that are not in the second; `intersect` keeps those in both. Here: countries with customers but no suppliers.

query.postgres:
select country from customers
except
select country from suppliers
order by country;

cards.after: 9 such countries.

cards.title: A query inside a query
cards.text: A query in brackets gives its answer to the outer query. Here the inner query works out the average price, and the outer one keeps the products above it.

query.postgres:
select product_name, unit_price
from products
where unit_price > (
  select avg(unit_price)
  from products
)
order by unit_price desc,
  product_id;

cards.after: 25 products cost more than the average.

cards.title: IN with a list from a query
cards.text: `in (select …)` checks a value against a list that another query makes. Here: the customers with at least one order whose freight is over 500.

query.postgres:
select company_name
from customers
where customer_id in (
  select customer_id
  from orders
  where freight > 500
)
order by customer_id;

cards.after: 8 customers.
cards.tip: `exists (select …)` asks the same question: is there at least one such row?

cards.title: Changing the type
cards.text: `cast(x as type)` turns a value into another type. Here: the date and time into just a date, and the freight into a whole number.

query.postgres:
select order_date,
  cast(order_date as date)
    as order_day,
  freight,
  cast(freight as integer)
    as whole
from orders
order by order_id;
query.mysql:
select order_date,
  cast(order_date as date)
    as order_day,
  freight,
  cast(freight as signed)
    as whole
from orders
order by order_id;

cards.tip: PostgreSQL also writes it `order_date::date`. MySQL knows only `cast`.
cards.mysqlText: `cast(x as type)` turns a value into another type. Here: the date and time into just a date, and the freight into a whole number (`signed`).
cards.mysqlTip: In MySQL a whole number is `signed`; PostgreSQL says `integer` and also has the short form `x::integer`.

cards.title: Tidying text
cards.text: Data typed by people is messy. `trim` cuts the spaces at the ends, `lower` writes in small letters, `nullif(x, '')` turns an empty text into NULL.

query.postgres:
select trim('  Alice  ') as name,
  lower('ALICE@MAIL.COM')
    as email,
  nullif('', '') as phone;

cards.after: Clean values, ready to compare and to count.

cards.title: Finding repeats
cards.text: To find values that appear more than once, group by them and keep the groups with `having count(*) > 1`. Here: cities with several customers.

query.postgres:
select city, count(*) as customers
from customers
group by city
having count(*) > 1
order by city;

cards.after: 10 cities have more than one customer.

cards.title: Pages with OFFSET
cards.text: To show page 3 with 5 rows on a page, skip two pages (`offset 10`) and take 5 (`limit 5`). Sort by something unique, like the id, so pages never overlap.

query.postgres:
select product_id, product_name
from products
order by product_id
limit 5 offset 10;

cards.after: Products 11 to 15.

cards.title: Continue after the last row
cards.text: On big tables `offset` gets slow: the skipped rows are still read. Instead, remember the last id shown and ask for the rows after it.

query.postgres:
select product_id, product_name
from products
where product_id > 15
order by product_id
limit 5;

cards.after: The next page, without reading the first 15 rows.
